props.title: The Mortal Storm
props.initialSlug: Love and defiance in Nazi Germany tear family apart

sections.content: The Mortal Storm (1940) stands as one of Hollywood's earliest and boldest anti-Nazi films, released while America was still officially neutral in WWII. MGM's brave production starred Margaret Sullavan and James Stewart as lovers torn apart by the rise of fascism in Germany. The film's depiction of Nazi persecution of Jewish professors and intellectuals proved so controversial that it was banned in Germany and caused MGM to be boycotted in all Axis-controlled territories. It shares thematic DNA with Casablanca (1942) and Watch on the Rhine (1943) in showing how fascism destroys families and forces ordinary people to take moral stands.

sections.content: Director Frank Borzage, known for romantic melodramas like 7th Heaven (1927), brings his humanist touch to this political story. Rather than focus solely on grand political themes, he shows fascism's poison through intimate family dynamics - brothers turning against brothers, children rejecting parents. The film's most devastating scene shows Nazi students burning books while singing patriotic songs, a chilling sequence that proved prophetic. Mrs. Miniver (1942) would later use similar domestic drama to show fascism's impact on ordinary families.

The film's technical achievements are notable for 1940. The skiing chase sequence near the end required innovative camera work and remains thrilling today. Frank Morgan (best known as the Wizard in The Wizard of Oz (1939)) delivers a powerful performance as the Jewish professor who refuses to bend his scientific principles to Nazi ideology. His death scene is handled with remarkable restraint for the era, making it all the more impactful. SUBHEAD: Early Anti-Fascist Cinema

sections.content: The Mortal Storm belongs to a crucial cluster of pre-war anti-fascist films including Confessions of a Nazi Spy (1939) and Four Sons (1940). These films faced enormous pressure from isolationists and the Hays Office to tone down their political messages. Some studios still had business interests in Germany and feared losing that market. The film's forthright condemnation of Nazism, while not naming Hitler directly, showed remarkable courage. Its box office success helped pave the way for more explicit anti-Nazi films like Mission to Moscow (1943).
